utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Just two housekeeping matters before we call the next witness. The first one is that the Chamber has received a motion for safe conduct for Witness MM-121, and what we just want to raise with you, Mr. Milovancevic, for the Defence, is that the Chamber is not yet in possession of the 92 bis statement of this witness. I don't know whether the Prosecution has a -- has it, but the Chamber doesn't and it looks like this witness is going to be coming to testify very soon. What is the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I know, we are expecting that witness on Thursday, and we'll try to resolve the matter as soon as possible, but I can't tell you anything at present. I can't really answer your question now until I check it out with my colleagues on the Defence team and I'll do that as soon as possible. But quite certainly, the witness, according to the information we have, will not be appearing before Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is true, but the point is just that we don't have to receive the statement just as the witness appears. I would imagine the Prosecution, if they haven't received it yet, they also need to use that statement to prepare. The Chamber also needs the statement to prepare. And if I'm not mistaken, there are times when the Prosecution wants to respond to the statement, to have certain things struck out or amended or whatever. So we need time to do that. Okay? So what I'm suggesting, therefore, is that if you can talk to your team at the next break so that they can investigate this, and it would be nice if maybe by sometime today you can give us an idea when to expect the statement. Okay? I don't know whether Mr. Whiting for the Prosecution has anything to add on that this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just that we have not received the statement. We have repeatedly requested it from the Defence, and Your Honour is correct that we would like to have it, and so we would be grateful for any indication as to when it might be coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. For the first time today I hear a voice coming out this way as we speak. Is there an open -- an open microphone somewhere? Am I the only one who hears it? There it goes. Okay. That's fine. The next point was -- relates to the Prosecution's motion to exclude the military expert's report of the Defence. I know that the parties are still exchanging documents with regard to that motion, but because of a request made in that motion that the Defence be asked to give a -- a response, the Chamber would like to give some order, oral order, on that request only. And it goes as follows: The Trial Chamber is seized of the Prosecution's motion to exclude certain sections of the military expert report of Milisav Sekulic filed yesterday 2nd November 2006. The Trial Chamber notes that the Prosecution have requested an expedited Defence response to this motion. Thank you so much. It's off now. The Trial Chamber finds that it is in the interests of justice, particularly having regard to the scheduled date for the close of the Defence case, that an expedited response be filed by the Defence. However, the Trial Chamber finds that the Prosecution's requested date of Monday, the 6th November is too short a deadline. The Trial Chamber therefore orders the Defence to file any response to the Prosecution's motion by no later than 4 p.m. on Thursday, the 9th November 2006. Okay. We can call in the next witness, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We are receiving something on the English channel.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. The microphone was on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, are you able to give us the name of the next witness and we can be writing it down while we are waiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the next witness is Dragana Knezevic, Dragana Knezevic will be coming into court -- Dragan Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As the lead counsel in the Defence team, I'm going to conduct your examination today, and before we go on to your CV and asking you questions I'd like to ask you one thing. Since you and I speak the same language, would you please make pauses between my question and your answer, to facilitate the work of the interpreters. And I should also like to ask you if possible to speak as slowly as possible for the same reasons.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But might I just say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Since I speak quickly, my natural speech is fast, please slow me down when I go to fast and I'll do my best to speak as slowly as possible, although it's not in my nature to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us your full name and surname and your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Knezevic, the 2nd of January 1962.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where were you born? And what ethnicity are you and what religion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Cetina, Knin municipality, and I'm a Serb and I'm Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What education have you had and where have you worked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I completed secondary school of internal affairs in Zagreb and I worked as a policeman doing patrol work in Zagreb, in the Crnomerec police station until 1983. In 1983, I moved to Djordjiceva Street to join the crime and drugs department there and in 1985 I moved to Knin to the police station of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: You're well come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you came to move to Knin and what work you were engaged in, in the Knin police station, what was your job there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I asked to be transferred from Zagreb to solve my accommodation problem. That is to say I didn't have adequate accommodation in Zagreb so I asked to be transferred to Knin. That is why I moved. And I worked in the patrol section of Knin, on the beat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were born in the village of Cetina. Can you tell us where that village is located in relation to Knin, how big is it, what is the composition of the inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The village is southeast of Knin, in the direction of Sinj. The village -- most of the inhabitants, 98 per cent, in fact, were Orthodox. The total number of inhabitants was 1500 or 600, not more than that. There were 270 households roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, since we are discussing this topic, what the nearest neighbouring villages are?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The neighbouring village on the left is Kosola [phoen] and Vrlika. Then Ciljane [phoen] is in front and Bosna on the right, and the village of Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you a little bit, Mr. Milovancevic? Was this witness not supposed to be 92 bis fully?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it says in my notes that this is a viva voce witness. That's why I set off in the way I did. Perhaps there was a misunderstanding because there were a number of people named Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're right. I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. Thank you. I feel better now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said you were educated in Zagreb and that you worked in Zagreb in the police force and after that, that you moved to Knin and worked for the police force there. Can you tell us up to 1990, how would you describe interethnic relations? And when I say that, I mean interethnic relations in the police force, the policemen, the Serbs, the Croats and others on the police force?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you couldn't notice any difference in ethnic affiliation. It did not gain expression in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: We all thought as one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What were the interethnic relations in your village, and in Knin, when you arrived there to take up your work from Zagreb, up until 1990?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Knin and the surrounding villages, the villages of the municipality, the interethnic relations were extremely proper. Great respect and tolerance for each other, a lot of understanding, people helped each other, they would go to each other's feast days, holidays, festivities, they would socialise, and it was a pleasure to work in a place like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did those relations change at any point in time and what was the basic reason for that, if they did?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the relations became disturbed in 1989, as far as I remember. In 1989, the reason why the relationships became disturbed and upset was the campaign launched by the Croatian Democratic Party, which introduced unrest among the people with the slogans it put out and its calls for a sort of Croatian state that they had envisaged in that time. I don't know what kind of state they envisaged because it was still Yugoslavia at that time, but fear was instilled in the people, fear of these rallies that were being held, demonstrations, and so on. The various slogans put out, the graffiti on the walls that appeared. You found slogans in the media, newspapers, everywhere where there were Croatian inhabitants. I can't say that this is true of all the Croatian inhabitants. They were extremists mostly, aided and abetted by the newly established powers that be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember when the first multi-party elections were held in Croatia just briefly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I do. But I can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after those elections, this situation as you described it, did it deteriorate or improve?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The situation became worse from one day to the next. We tried to calm the situation down by holding various negotiations, talking to people that we knew, that we had gone to school with, to ask for understanding on their part, but all to no avail because the official authorities in Croatia were not interested in peace. And that wasn't my own feeling, that was what the population over there felt. Not only the Serbs but the Croats, too, shared that view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you tried to calm the situation down.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You were working as a policeman, so how did you go about trying to calm the situation down? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I was working in Knin four or five years before the war, and that's enough time to get to know the population of a municipality like Knin which is a small municipality. I was good friends both with Croats and Serbs. I went to attend their feast days, weddings, birthdays, and so on. There were no tensions. It didn't matter that the person was a Croat or a Serb. And negotiations were held in 1990, in August, the month of August, the police forces from Solina, special units commanded by Romac Ivica, who was a schoolmate of mine from Zagreb. We went to school for four years together. I went to Zagreb, he went to the military academy in Belgrade, and then he became commander of the special units in Solin and on the 20th of August, round about that date --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, witness, please. We'll come to that in due course. Thank you, you've answered my question. Now I'll just move on, and we'll come to what you were saying in due course. You said you, "took part in the negotiations and we tried to calm the situation down and the official authorities were not in favour or didn't want peace." That's what you said. Now, how can you say that? What are the grounds for you saying that? You were a policeman and now you are presenting us with that view?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. Your Honour, I would object on the fact that this issue of negotiations and things like that, as far as I can see, it's not on the 65 ter summary. It's also pre-1991, although it's not one of the specific topics that was listed by the Chamber the other day, but I would object on that ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I've actually had my finger on the button to intervene myself to ask if -- is this not part of the background information that we agreed yesterday or the day before that we can skip and get to the real issues that go to the acts and conduct of the accused? We already know, as the Chamber, the position of the Defence on these topics. We know the position of the Prosecution on these topics. We note that. So maybe if you can just move on to the charges themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am fully cognizant of what you just said. I am bearing that in mind. I just wish very briefly to deal with one topic and that is the behaviour of the members of the SUP of Knin, and the Prosecution claims that Mr. Martic is responsible for their attitude and relationship towards the population and the situation, and so on. So it was only along those lines that I wished to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't mention those things because that's part of the testimony you want to extract from the witness. You know? I don't know why you keep doing this, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I won't deal with that topic any more. So I withdraw the question, my last question. I didn't wish to suggest or lead the witness in any way. I just wanted to respond to the remarks made by the Prosecution, because Mr. Martic is being held for everything that a living being can be held responsible for and stands accused of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please stop. Will you deal with the objection, then, by your learned friend that what you are testify -- what you are eliciting from the witness at this stage is not on the 65 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the statement summary, in paragraph 4, it says that the witness took part in talks with the Croatian side in which they agreed, et cetera, et cetera, to de-block the roads, the JNA positions and so on. So if the witness took part in the talks, I assume that that is the subject that I'm dealing with now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suppose it's conceivable that I'm mistaken but when you -- you read the summary this is talking about Kijevo and the events in Kijevo in August of 1991. Not 1990, which seemed to be what we were talking about now. And I think it was quite clear that the witness has been discussing August 1990. It's a year earlier than what appears to be these talks with the Croatian side on which it was agreed that the blockade be lifted. Apparently it's referring to a blockade of Kijevo. I don't see how that could possibly refer to August of 1990, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that, Your Honour. Yes, I accept that objection, and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you refer to this disruption of relations that used to be good, can you tell us how was this manifested in 1990? What manifestation of forms did it have, did it assume, in your place, where you came from, on the ground?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, your learned friend says according to your statement, this witness's statement talks of relations in August of 1991 in Kijevo, not 1990 in Knin. Now you're going back to 1990 in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we informed our colleagues from the OTP today by additional information that this witness would be also dealing with such subjects as the signing of the petition in June in 1990, then another petition as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why didn't you say so when you objected, Mr. Milovancevic? You should have told him that. That was the answer. Then he could have dealt with it. Instead you accept the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took the objection to mean, Your Honours -- I thought that he was objecting to the witness's participation in the negotiations, that that is what his objection specifically referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: His objection is you are leading evidence on a period and place that you have not mentioned in the 65 ter statement. That's the objection. Unless I misunderstand the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think slightly, Your Honour. Maybe I wasn't clear. Mr. Milovancevic is quite righting that my specific objection was that the -- whatever negotiations might have been in August of 1990, that was not on the 65 ter summary. Where it might have been confusing is I also mentioned that all these events are pre-1991 and I referred to Your Honour's decision earlier in the week, but -- it's true that relations in Knin are in the 65 ter summary, just so that's clear, nothing about negotiations or something like that but the general topic of relations is in the 65 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So he may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If Your Honour is inclined to hear more evidence about relations in 1990, then he's entitled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber is not [inaudible] earlier in the week, but Mr. Milovancevic insists so I don't know what to do here. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can I now move on with your permission to some very concrete things?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you know anything about a petition that was signed by the members of the police station in Knin? When was this and what was this about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know about that petition. I was a signatory of it also. I believe that was in June 1990. I'm not quite sure but I believe that that was the date. And this petition was signed after our colleagues from Zadar had also signed a petition and referred it to all institutions in the former Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Croatia, to the SUPs, to the Ministries of Justice, to all the factors in the state. They were revolting because of the emblems --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I will have to interrupt you at this point. When we speak about this petition by policemen in the station in Knin, can you tell us what the basic reason for that petition was? What was it that you wished to achieve by it, in your view?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The reason for the petition were the emblems that were being offered to us by the new Croatian authorities, which, actually, conjured up images of the dark past of the Second World War in our minds, in which past many people had lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether that petition -- first of all to whom was this petition addressed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It was addressed to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, and to the federal Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry of Defence, the SUPs in Croatia. Some supported it, others didn't, but those were the addressees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the attitude of the policemen employed in the Knin police station vis-a-vis that petition? How many signed it, how many didn't, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: 90 per cent of them signed it. Some were absent because they had -- they declined to sign it because they thought that perhaps they would remain without employment if they did, but most of them did sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was in July 1990 that a petition was, in fact, published in the press. Do you know which petition that was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: That is the petition which we signed in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you want to achieve as policemen by that petition? What was your objective?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Our objective at that time was primarily to prevent any blood letting, which could be felt in the air. The people could feel it. The policemen could feel it. It was hovering in the air and people were expecting things to happen and things did happen later. As the state of Yugoslavia existed at the time, we were loyal to that state at the time, and we couldn't accept those emblems because those emblems were precisely offering that -- this something else which indeed happened later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the petition signed by the policemen in Knin, there was also a petition signed by policemen in Zadar. What kind of a petition was that? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know. The petition in Zadar was signed by almost 150 members of the regular police force of the then state, many people who were professionally trained to discharge those duties. That was a mixed composition. In fact, the ratio was 70 to 30 per cent. 70 per cent of them were Croats and 30 were Croats [as interpreted] and a total of 150 signed the petition and they also were protesting against the evil that was in the offing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the usher please deliver this document to the Trial Chamber, to our learned colleagues from the OTP, to the witness, and we also have copies for the interpreters. The translation, Your Honours, is after the B/C/S text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you read at the very top of this document, who is this letter addressed to, who is it sent by, and who are all the addressees to whom it is to be delivered?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: "Open letter of the policemen of SUP Zadar to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreters still haven't got their copy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So: "Open letter of the policemen of SUP Zadar to the president of the Republic of Croatia, to the government of the Republic of Croatia, to the Minister of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia, to the Minister of National Defence of the Republic of Croatia, and to all the Secretariats of the Interior in the Republic of Croatia. To the Presidency of the SFRY. To the Federal Executive Council. To the Federal Secretariat of the Interior's secretary and to the Federal Secretary of National Defence."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: You said that I should read the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: No, thank you. That will suffice. Please turn to the very end of this text. That is page 3 in the B/C/S version, which bears the date and the place where this letter was drafted and it is followed by a signature. Can you read for us where this letter was written and on what day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: In Zadar, on the 5th of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this letter, I'm going to turn your attention to two or three paragraphs. The second paragraph on the first page. "Why, after the order of the MUP of the Republic of Croatia on activating reserve police forces, why were weapons and ammunition distributed to people who had not originally been designated to serve on the reserve force and who had not previously gone through the compulsory checks? Why were these members of the police reserve force [without uniforms] as well as the newly admitted and trained-in-a-hurry policemen allowed to bring long barrelled and short barrelled weapons and ammunitions to their houses, if it is known that they do not have any legal authorisation whatsoever to undertake any kind of police actions and thus also no right to possess weapons?" Then the fifth paragraph, I'm going to read for you the fifth and the sixth paragraphs on this page. "Why has the special purposes unit of this SUP been disbanded? It was a nationally mixed unit and regular in every respect, [declared to be the best special purposes unit in the whole Croatia]." This last part was in brackets. "After that, this unit was created again exclusively from the newly accepted policemen of Croatian nationality, the great majority of whom were over 25, meaning that they did not meet one of the basic requirements for the creation of such a unit. Some of them are not sufficiently qualified, some of them have finished only primary school." And then the last paragraph: "Why have policemen of Serbian nationality been excluded from all the above-mentioned by which differentiation on a national basis is being done between members of the service without any grounds and justification. This causes justified revolt, doubt, dissatisfaction, uncertainty and distrust among personnel of both Serbian and Croatian nationalities." Do you see this text, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does this text which is in this -- on these pages, does it correspond to reality, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It fully corresponds to reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I propose, Your Honours, that this document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you have read it all, virtually all. Do you still need it in evidence after you've read it? The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there are 142 signatures and there is more text that I did not wish to burden the Trial Chamber with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 1005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the reaction was after you sent this letter from the Knin police station? Was there any reaction to it? Were there any consequences that you had to bear? Were any measures taken?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we were laid off, all of us. Those were the direct consequences, as far as we were concerned, the members of the SUP Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Milovancevic, was the witness one of the signatories? Could you establish that? I'm just asking because the witness said something about "we".

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has explained that he signed the letter from the Knin station and I'm going to ask him about this other one referred to in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, you have explained that you signed the police petition from Knin. Were you a signatory of this petition as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. But this one we just received by way of information. We did not sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In order to clarify things to the full, who signed this other petition that we just saw now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Our colleagues from the Zadar SUP did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So I'm not mistaken to say that members of the SUP of the Secretariat of internal affairs in Zadar, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about barricades? When did they appear, Mr. Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm not sure how Your Honour wants me to deal with this but this is a specifically mentioned topic from which the Trial Chamber advised the Defence to refrain from leading evidence. It's at transcript page 10471, line 14, the barricades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic? Let's try to move on, Mr. Milovancevic, on to the charges. I think this -- the question of barricades, we indicated that we have heard a lot about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the objection is apparently logical but it is not grounded. I'm not trying to deal with the subject of barricades as such. What I'm interested in is a specific situation in the village of Civljani where the witness was, and he knows how the special police forces, Croatian police forces, acted on that particular occasion in 1990 so that this is not covered by the instruction of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why don't you ask him clearly about that, about the situation in the village of Civljani rather than about barricades?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right, Your Honour. I shall rephrase my question along those lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What do you know in relation to events at the barricades in the village of Civljani? Do you know when that was approximately and what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of that. I know about it. But I will have to go into some detail to explain to the Trial Chamber. I believe that it was the 20th of August. But don't hold me to that. I think it was on the 20th of August at 2315 hours, it was 1990, yes, 1990, I apologise, the 20th of August, 1990 at 2315 hours in the evening. I was coming from -- back from work from the second shift in Knin, and I reached Civljani at about quarter to 11. There were about 15 to 20 people standing around next to a shop. Some of them were armed with hunting rifles, hunting weapons. They had trophy weapons, we are talking about 1990, that's the year, and at 2315 hours, you could hear somebody over the megaphone. It was night time. And as that part of the road is surrounded by hills, it sounded terrible. And the people dispersed when they heard this megaphone just a little after 11.00 at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you, Witness, but in order to find your way on the map, if you look at page 32 of the map, the atlas, you have Vrlika, Kijevo, Cetina, and the other villages on both sides of the road, and that's the area that the witness is referring to now. Continue, please, Witness.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: There was a voice which warned, "Take down the barricade," over the megaphone, the barricades and obstacles on the road. There were none but the people were there. Then the next time over the megaphone there was a voice saying, "Take away the barricade or else we'll resort to other measures." And the third time it said, "I hereby order that the barricade be removed." I saw that the situation was serious and I happened to be there. I recognised the voice of Romac Ivica, my school friend. I went out on to the road and I shouted to him, "I'm coming to talk to you."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, before you proceed you didn't give us a grid number and letter for page 32 of the map, in relation to the location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It is page 31, and it is C 2, the grid reference is C 2. In the middle of the atlas, the map. At the level of -- it is between Knin and Drnis on the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please continue, witness, and I apologise for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I went to see Mr. Romac, went up to Mr. Romac. I recognised me -- he recognised me, I recognised him. And when I asked him, "What are you doing there?" He said, "And what are you doing here?" And I said, "I'm doing the same as you." At that point in time -- well, this exchange went on for just a few minutes. And then somebody shot, fired a shot from the left side, as far as I was able to notice. And then shooting started in a circle around us. We didn't know who was doing the shooting. There was panic among the people. You could hear them rushing up the hill, Kozjak hill. It was night-time, so you could hear all this. And in that shooting, my colleague, my former school colleague, said, "What's all this about?" And I said, "I don't know." And I really didn't. I just said that he and I were in the same situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will do. Just stop there. Now, when you started talking to him, up until that moment, did you discuss why they had come, what their task was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked my school friend, my colleague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why who had come? You asked him, "Did you discuss why they had come." Who are the "they" and their task?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll hear through the witness's answers who the "they" were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us who those others were, the "they," and who this colleague or friend, school friend of yours, was representing when he spoke over the megaphone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Romac Ivica was my colleague. He was commander of the special units from Solin, Solina. When I asked him what his intention was in coming there, he said, "To remove the barricade." I said, "The barricade is no problem because there is no barricade. And what next?" And he said, "It depends on the orders. I understand police work. Orders are issued by a superior authority." And that's when the shooting started. My colleague asked me what I could do about that, to calm the situation down. And I said, "Hand over that megaphone of yours." The megaphone was in a Landrover, the man who handed me the megaphone -- I got into the Landrover and I asked the people to stop shooting. They didn't react at all. The first time when I said this they didn't react. When I said it a second time, I repeated, "Do not shoot." And the third time I introduced myself and I told them not to shoot, that it was Dragan Knezevic talking to them, addressing them, and then the shooting stopped. And then my colleague Romac withdrew his men, the men who had been deployed in a firing line. I did not know that until then. Buses were there. There were 60 people there who were fully equipped. This special unit, they had flak jackets, helmets, snipers, automatic weapons, they had everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: May I stop you there? You said that they were people equipped with a full BK. Could you tell us what you mean by BK?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: They are combat kits. BK are combat kits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So these were with specials, members of the special unit from Solin, and who did they belong to? Whose command were they under?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: They were under the command of the SUP of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The buses started moving along the road without their lights on because it was night time. I used the megaphone again and told the people that heard me and who knew me that I would go in my car in front of them to Vrlika and I said, "If you're going to shoot, shoot at me." That's what I said to them. And then I went to the police station in Vrlika with this colleague of mine, this man named Romac and he invited me to have a whiskey. We stayed there for about an hour. So I went to their police station in Vrlika. The man did withdraw his men and we continued to cooperate very well. We held negotiations to quell the people in Civljani and the other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that witness but since you mentioned these negotiations in that village and the other two villages, now this good cooperation during the negotiations it was period is this in view of -- relating to these three villages?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: 1990 to 1991 until the redarstvenici forces arrived in Knin, when everything changed and the situation deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a question to ask before we move on. The people who were shooting, were they the people, the 15 to 20 people that you found standing at the shop or were they part of this unit of -- that was travelling in buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Those were the locals, those 15 or 20 people, and around them there were all the villagers. They were locals of the villages but I don't know who. They were shooting out of fear, because to hear a megaphone at 2315 hours, that's a terrible sound to behold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They were the people who were shooting, the 15 to 20 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, whether it was one of them, I can't say. I was with Mr. Romac negotiating so I can't confirm who actually did the shooting. Because behind us there was a Croatian village, there was shooting coming from there as well, from that location so I can't really say. Everybody was shooting, the Orthodox people were shooting, the Croats were shooting, and we were in the centre holding talks, negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The shooting didn't come from your friend's unit, the people in the bus, in the buses? Didn't come from those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They were distributed in a line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And linked to that question that Judge Moloto just asked you let's try to clarify one more point. When this shooting started, was it shooting at you and the policemen you were talking to or was it something else again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody was wounded or killed. It was mostly shooting up in the air, I assume, because none of us, nobody was wounded or injured or killed while I was talking to Romac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did you establish what the assignment was in talking to Romac and others? What was the assignment of this special unit made up of the 60 men you mentioned with the combat kits and all the rest of it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't know what the assignment of that unit was but we assumed that they were to advance towards Knin. That was my assumption. The next day, we learnt that in Drnis, the police had thrown down their arms and did not wish to attack Knin, and this was a synchronised action which was an abortive one. But we learned that the next day when our colleagues from Drnis arrived, when they threw down their arms and left the SUP. But the previous night we didn't know about any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These police forces from Drnis Zadar and Sinj, whose forces were they, under whose authority?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after this event, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: After this occurrence, I and Mr. Romac, that is my colleague, Romac, took it upon ourselves, and we informed Mr. Martic about this, to negotiate with the people, to try and calm the situation down, and he lent his support. We went to the village of Lelasi and I had another colleague in that village. He occupies a high-ranking post in Croatia today. We went to his house, Mr. Romac and I did, and we talked to the locals there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. Can you tell us the village of Lelasi, what ethnic composition is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It's a 100 per cent Croatian village, Croatians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now tell us what you talked about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: We discussed the security and safety of the people, to see what was going on, what was bothering them, how to reduce tensions, how to calm the situation and the people down, and the people accepted this. They said they were in favour of law and order and peace, for people and goods to be able to move around freely, that there should be no check-points or control points along the roads, the army held a buffer zone in the area. We went to the village of Civljani and also talked there, to the locals there, and they are exclusively an Orthodox population. I, and Mr. Romac talked to the people there. They said they it were just interested in having quiet time and going about their work so we did well there too. We came upon a good reception.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, in this village, Lelasi and Civljani, when was this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: That was in August 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, what happened next?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: We visited the village of Kijevo next. There was a larger meeting there, there was Romac, there was Zeljko Golisija from Split. He was the chief of SUP Split. And president of the local commune, Joso Juric-Orlic was there. Petar Alvir was another man. And another colleague who happened to come by and joined in the meeting. In Kijevo we discussed having the situation return to normal, that people could travel to see Sinj and Knin normally. What happened on one occasion was that a bus from Knin to Cetina was stoned along the route. I drew their attention to that. Mr. Joso Juric said that that was something that the children had done, and I said, "They are your children, children from Kijevo, sir." And I said, "They are our children, too, which have to be better brought up, if they are not brought up already." And he said, "Well, I can do nothing about the children." Any way this happened several times. We discussed others matters at the meeting, too, which were not linked to the war. But the situation became more complicated when some 300 people gathered together calling for arms, and they were in front of the school, the school building in Kijevo. Also at the meeting there was a teacher named Varnica - I don't know what his first name was - and he said, "They are asking for arms," and I had just arrived to the negotiations. He said, "You're provoking us." I said "No, I came to your village with no weapons, well intentioned, I wanted to talk to the representatives of the village and the police to calm the situation." Mr. Romac went outside, saw that the situation had come to a head, and that they were calling for bloodshed. We made -- we passed through this group, went to our car, and took off. Thanks to Mr. Romac, we were able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the establishment of the police station in Kijevo, the MUP of Croatia police station, how it was set up in Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The police station, Postaja as it was called in Kijevo, suddenly emerged one morning. There was no need to set up a police station in Kijevo which numbered at the time 150 men, for a small village with 1500 or 600 inhabitants. People lived in Zagreb, in Split and so on. And that's when the problems started, that's when the big problems started. As far as I was concerned it was a sort of army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us where -- who did the SUP of Kijevo come under?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The SUP of the Republic of Croatia, that is to say the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia. I think the headquarters were in Split, perhaps, or Sibenik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who made up this police station in Kijevo or police department in Kijevo and do you know what kind of equipment those people had?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to the man who was commander in Kijevo, Mr. Vucic. I talked to him, and when they entered Kijevo to set up that police station, they put up check-points at the entrance and exit to Kijevo on three roads around Kijevo and they controlled the whole area, and mistreated the people. They mistreated small children. I know about several instances. Mr. Vucic had on a camouflage uniform, he was wearing a camouflage uniform, which didn't exist where we were from at that time. Whose it was, I don't know. He had short-barrelled weapons at the -- a short-barrel weapon at the negotiations but the others had weapons and flak jackets, bullet-proof vests. Mr. Vucic was born in Kasteli. I know that in talking to him. Mr. Romac attended those negotiations as did a representative of the army, Babic Dusin was his name. The object of the negotiations was to lift the blockade on the Vrlika-Knin road or Knin-Sinj-Vrlika road, because the village of Kijevo cut off all communication with our basic municipality, that of Kijevo, and we were under siege. We were encircled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you said cut off all communication, who do you mean when you say us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I mean the villages of Cetina and Civljani, because I lived there and I couldn't go to work because the blockade lasted for a month. And this was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before we take our break, I shall ask you another question. Was this road through Kijevo the only road? Couldn't one take another perhaps longer and safer and passable road?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No. This was the only road. One would only walk across the hill, over the hill, or take the road on the other side via Sinj which we couldn't do because we were blockaded. We were surrounded. We had no exit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These negotiations which involved the commander of this police station, where were they held?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: They were held in a tent right on the outskirts of Kijevo. So at the very entrance to Kijevo, in a military tent which was make shift facility offered by the army and we agreed that the road communication would be left to the army and the army was in charge of that particular section of the road, and was to see to it that there was no bloodshed, that there should be no clashes between the villagers of the surrounding villages. So the army was in control of the three buffer zones separating the people in the villages where emotions were already running very high.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These three buffer zones were between what villages, whose villages?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Between Orthodox and Croatian villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For how long did those buffer zones exist and did they function? Did the JNA manage to perform its duty, that particular task?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It was -- they were honoured, they were respected for a while. We all abided by them, and after a while, Mr. Vucic -- Mr. Vucic also respected them for a while and allowed communication to unfold, but at night nobody could use the road except the army, possibly some people could go but with escorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This last thing which you said, does that mean that it was only possible to pass through Kijevo if accompanied by the army, if escorted by the army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that now is a convenient time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. We will take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, the issue we discussed before the break was the situation in Kijevo, and the police station there. You mentioned the buffer zones set up by the JNA. Which part of the year was that, do you recall, or at least which year it was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: That was 1991, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that for a while the agreement was honoured and that Kijevo could be passed through. How long did it last, this period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: 20 days at the most. Then it was violated by the police force in Kijevo under the command of Mr. Gucic [phoen], the so-called redarstvenici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What does it mean when you say that the agreement was violated by the police officers in Kijevo? How did it manifest itself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: This meant that again they controlled all the roads and mistreated the civilians who went past along the road from Vrlika to Knin and the road went through Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us which civilians were being mistreated? And I mean their ethnicity. And how were they mistreated?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Specifically, when a person came down the road in a car with their family, the forces there would force them to get out of the car, search the car, open the boot, detain them unnecessarily, as if searching for something. That's what mistreatment meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the JNA action at Kijevo, when it took place, and how it came about? Or rather why it came about? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The JNA action on Kijevo took place in 1991. One day ahead of the action a tragedy occurred which shook all of us deeply, in particular the residents of my village. Mr. Dragisa Vranjes worked in Switzerland. He was taken off a bus on his way home. He ended up in the prison in Sibenik. Dragisa Vranjes, before the attack on Kijevo, was brutally murdered in Sibenik. This was proved later on. He was killed in prison. He was the -- resident of my village. People heard stories about it through their different family ties, it doesn't really matter, to the effect that it was the residents of Kijevo who were behind this, or rather the police officers who were working in Sibenik and hailed from Kijevo. The day before the attack on Kijevo, carried out by the JNA, the JNA forces came under attack in the area of Kosori by the police force of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but it wasn't clear to me from the question that this is what was intended to get at. But none of this about this person's death in prison the day before, the day before the attack the JNA -- the attack on Kijevo the JNA forces came under attack in Kosovoj [phoen], none of this is on the 65 ter summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in paragraph 5 of the summary, it says that after the agreement, Kijevo was blocked again and several Serbs were killed in the month of August of 1991 and the JNA carried out the action in order to lift the blockades and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have a copy of the 65 ter summary? Because what it says is "Soon" -- it talks about the -- whatever these negotiations were. "Soon afterward, the roadblock was put again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This is paragraph 4, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, then it goes into paragraph 5. Several Serbs were killed. In August 1991 the JNA undertook an action to lift the blockade. Now, that's different. Now the suggestion is that it was an action in response to someone who died in prison or it was a response to an attack the day before. That's not in here, Your Honour. I would also mention that none of this was ever put to Prosecution witnesses. It wasn't until the last witness who talked about Kijevo was the first time we heard about this idea, that maybe there was an attack on the JNA right before and now we hear it again in this witness's testimony although it's not in the 65 ter summary. It's impossible for to us prepare for cross-examination when we don't know what the witness is going to say about something, besides the fact he's going to talk about Kijevo in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is upheld. While I'm talking, Mr. Milovancevic, you have 20 minutes to go. This witness is scheduled for three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will finish within five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the information mentioned now were testified to in great detail by a general who was called to testify here. Therefore, the Prosecutor cannot say that he was not prepared for this when this was the subject of evidence which lasted five hours here in front of the Trial Chamber, and I'm referring to General Djukic. And now, it's not that the witness stated that the murder of this person was the immediate cause of the attack. He merely relayed that particular incident which preceded the attack. May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you've raise issues here. You're saying General Djukic testified on this topic. That's not the point. The point is you've got to give your learned friends advanced warning on what your witnesses are going to testify on so that they can prepare. Now, it may very well be that General Djukic has testified on it. Did now they read what General Djukic said in preparation to cross-examine this witness? The answer is no because they say they haven't prepared on this point because it was not mentioned in your 65 ter summary. Proceed, Mr. Milovancevic. The objection is upheld, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will bear this in mind. However, for fairness's sake I have to say that in paragraph 3 of the summary, which is quite brief, I accept that, it says that the witness took part in the talks with the Croatian side where it had been agreed that the blockade be lifted and that the JNA remain in the area as a guarantor of the agreement. After that, it says that the blockade was lifted and several Serbs were killed. And this is what the witness is talking about right now. He is about to talk about the JNA action on Kijevo. At any rate, I accept and I have to accept your ruling and I will carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, can you tell us what, to your knowledge, the reason behind the JNA attack was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I can. The reason for the attack, or, rather, for the action of the army of Yugoslavia, the JNA, on Kijevo, was the fact that their forces were attacked near Kosori and Civljani where three people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that three people were killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who killed whom?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian police forces killed --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This is exactly what I objected to because it wasn't in the 65 ter summary and he's gone right back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black, when there is reference to several people being killed, can't they be mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, he said, "Can you tell us the reason behind the JNA attack?" The reason was that the -- was -- for the attack or rather for the action of the army was the fact that their forces were attacked near Kosori and Civljani where three people were killed but there is nothing about -- there is nothing here about an attack on Kosori or Civljani, much less connected, and say that that's the reason for the attack on Kijevo. There were two things, I objected earlier to the person who is -- apparently died in prison and then this other idea that there was an attack immediately preceding the Kijevo action which caused the Kijevo action. That's not in the 65 ter summary, Your Honour, and I think it's important. And it's something that they obviously knew about. They knew about the details. They could have told us. In fact, we received a supplementary information sheet today from the Defence at noon which says nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in August 1991, the JNA carried out an action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. The JNA had to go through Kijevo to reach its forces at Kosori because there was no other way to reach that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In that JNA action were there any people killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, none of them were killed or wounded. There were people captured, 60 uniformed people were captured in Kijevo, among whom there were two women.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How did you come to know that during the JNA action in Kijevo, 60 uniformed persons were taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Because I was contacted at the Kijevo police station to transport the people to Knin which I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us who told you to do that and what did you transport the prisoners with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who it was, a duty officer, who informed me there, and 40 persons were transported in a civilian bus and 22 in a military bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The persons who were captured, you said, were in uniform. What sort of uniform was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Camouflage uniform and they all had long weapons. They were with full combat gear. Not all of them had bullet-proof vests. Only 10 of them. This was their special squad at Kijevo that was part of these two platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you ferry the people to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Bozo Ceko and I took them over to the police station in Knin. From there, I believe they were taken to the southern barracks or I don't know where they were but they were taken over by the duty officer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Another important point, none of the people were mistreated, none of those who were taken prisoner at Kijevo. I can guarantee that. And one other thing: As we were taking them to Knin, Mr. Martic came to inspect and he told us, "Please make sure that none of the people are harmed or killed." And then my colleague Bozo Ceko asked him, well, why? And then he answered, "Well, these people have to be exchanged. They are prisoners."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what happened to the people captured in Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: None of them were residents of Kijevo. All of them hailed from Kasteli, and they were all exchanged quite soon, some 15 or 20 days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In the course of your duties in the police station in Knin, did you have occasion to get to know Mr. Martic as a colleague?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what his work ethic was and what his attitude towards people was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I can. Mr. Milan Martic was the sort of person who tried to solve the most difficult of problems through -- by looking at the funny side of things, sunny side of things, through humour, and I know that he solved matters as he went along. And he was the sort of person who did his job easily, with ease.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The last question: Do you know if he differentiated between people along ethnic, religious or any other bases?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I know of no such instances. I only know that regardless of ethnicity, he sought to assist people and that is how we were taught and brought up at the time, not to distinguish between people along any ethnic lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have completed my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, my name is Mr. Black. As you may have already gathered I'm one of the prosecutors on the case, so now it's my turn to ask you a few questions, okay? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: First of all on the topic of petitions, one thing, just so that I can get it clear, you said that the petition in Knin was followed -- excuse me, that it followed a similar petition in Zadar, but, in fact, the Knin petition came first in June or July of 1990 and then the Zadar one followed on later, around October of 1990. Is that the right chronology?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: This is written here when the petition in Zadar was and I know when the petition in Knin was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So if it says here the petition in Zadar -- actually, could we look at Exhibit 1005 briefly just so that I can have clarity on this from the witness? And we agree that the petition in Knin was in June or perhaps the beginning of July 1990, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's see if we can establish when the Zadar petition was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's dated the 5th of November 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. There is also -- just for the witness's edification, there is also a reference there. It says -- I can just read it out, we don't need to wait for it to come up. It says, "About 100 policemen, among whom there were ten Croats, requested answers to these and some other questions on the 22nd of October 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Does that help you remember, sir that it would have been the end of October or maybe the beginning of November, when the Zadar petition was done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wasn't it done on the 5th of November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you an accurate response to that question. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Dated the 5th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour, I wasn't clear whether this was the petition or whether this other thing that's referred to in October was the petition, and this was a different open letter but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My understanding is that on the 22nd of October, there was some kind of discussion with the leadership in Zadar and because maybe that discussion did not bear fruit, a petition was then drafted on the 5th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay, that makes sense to me, Your Honour and I think if we haven't gotten it right then certainly Mr. Milovancevic on redirect will clarify it. But I think that's fine for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, the Knin petition was followed by a meeting with Croatian authorities around the 5th of July 1990. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that Mr. Boljkovac attended this meeting at that time and Josko Moric [phoen] as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think that's the same meeting I was referring to. It's correct, isn't it, that those Croatian authorities actually required an escort in order to be able to get out of that meeting unharmed because a big crowd had gathered at the police station, et cetera, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, then, at that time, perhaps a large number of people assembled but no one asked for escort, nor was any escort necessary. I don't know about that. I was just a policeman. Perhaps some superior authorities or my superiors may have been asked for an escort. None was requested from me. So I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. You made that clear.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, as regards this petition, perhaps the date it bears is when it was addressed, whether it was sent to the different institutions which are indicated in the address, and it may have been signed before that date. That is quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay, but regardless of the specific day it was late -- it was later on, it was in the fall, sometime possible probably in October, right? Does that fit with your recollection as to when the Zadar petition was signed and that all happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I heard about the Zadar petition from my colleagues. Someone had obtained it and read it and it spread by word of mouth so that everybody knew about it - not only us at the police station - so that the people knew what it was about as well. I cannot give you a precise answer to that question. As regards the Knin one, yes, I can, because I am a signatory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay, very well. That's clear. Going back to the meeting at the beginning of July where Mr. Boljkovac and other people were there from the Croatian MUP or the Croatian authorities in any event, it was really after that point, after that meeting, that the police in Knin at least the Serb police in Knin no longer recognised the authority of the Croatian MUP, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: After the meeting in Knin, and I think that that is also a question for those who were my superiors at the time and not for me, and I believe that that Mr. Vujko was the secretary at the Knin SUP. Chief, the head, Mr. Slobodan Vujko.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually he arrived a little bit later, right? It was after the petition, some maybe a few weeks after the petition, that Slobodan Vujko became the chief of the Knin police station, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: What year are you referring to? 1990?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: 1990. I know for a fact that on the 17th of August he was at the police station and I cannot assert that that was the case before that. I know that he was there on the 17th of August and I can tell you how I know that, if you are interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No. That's fine. I don't think we need to go into detail on it. I want to go on to something else. And just so you know, based on one of the answers before, it's quite all right if you don't know the answer to one of my questions, you can always say -- you can agree with me or say no, but if you just don't know the answer it's quite all right to say you don't know, just so you know that. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I shall try to follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Around the same time, a little bit after the petition, is it correct or isn't it correct that there was also a leaflet going around Knin which identified eight Serb policemen who had not signed the petition? Do you remember that, remember seeing or hearing about that leaflet?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about this leaflet, but I know that people's names were called out, that people were pointed to. I was very -- on very good terms with those people who had not signed the petition including Stevan Trivic, who was a personal friend of mine, and it goes without saying that I wouldn't do anything against a friend, and we are still friends today. As for the leaflet I really don't know anything about it. I don't know that a leaflet was produced or written by anyone, and then Knin is a small place so one would have heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know anything about some of those people who you said -- there was -- talked about, the people who hadn't signed it. Did you know that some of those people were attacked and nearly killed by a mob outside the police station either on the 17th of August 1990 or perhaps a day or two after that? Did you hear about such an incident?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: That people were attacked? Those who declined to sign the petition? Is that what you're saying? Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Anyhow, some of those people who had not signed the petition were sort of threatened and nearly attacked or attacked or something like that around the 17th of August, did you hear about that at the police station? Or did you see it yourself?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: First of all I wasn't there. But no one was attacked physically, and as for any verbal attacks, you cannot forbid anyone to attack somebody else in that way. I know for a fact that there were no physical assaults and, as for verbal ones, that may have been the case. Verbal provocations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I interrupt? Witness could you repeat the name of your close friend, colleague, who was one of those who had not signed, Stevan or Stefan so and so? The one who I used -- who you are still in good terms with, on good terms with? What was his name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Stevan Trivic and Vlado Babic, two of them, in fact. And, in fact, Zivko Ognjenovic as well, and I'm on good terms with him as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Could you repeat these three names once more and then I'm satisfied, Stevan Trivic or -- with a V?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Trivic with a V.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Trivic or Strific?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: TRIVIC, Trivic with a V. Then Mr. Ognjenovic, Zivko Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you for the spelling of these names. Thank you very much. And Mr. Black, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, let me keep moving along. You said earlier that after this petition you said, "we were all laid off," and just so that I'm clear about that, in fact, Martic was -- Mr. Martic was suspended and three other people were suspended. But no one else was suspended or dismissed from their jobs on the basis of this petition; isn't that right? From Knin, I mean.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: We were all suspended, the entire force on the Knin police station, by a decision of the then president of the Republic of Croatia, Mr. Franjo Tudjman.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: A cable came, a telegram came that we were all dismissed, that our employment thenceforth terminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: After the petition, whether it was the 30th or the 31st, I can't be sure but in 1991, basically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in July, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were you suspended or were you dismissed? You've used the words "suspended" and you said "employment terminated forthwith." Were you suspended or were you dismissed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. We were dismissed. All of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
