utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic so did you all stop working then, when you were dismissed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So according to you, after the 30th or 31st of July there was no working police in Knin any more?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't working. Sorry. Actually, it wasn't functioning under the authority of the Republic of Croatia. It was not under the authority of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But there is still police doing work, you and the other policemen in Knin, you were no longer under the authority of the Republic of Croatia, but you continued to do police duties, is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Earlier you -- you -- you spoke about this event or I think in August of 1990 and you said that you were trying to calm the situation and that you went to Mr. Martic and he approved of that. Do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me just show you a clip, if we could -- oh, actually we may have to wait a minute. I forgot to tell our case manager that we have a Sanction clip. I can come back to it in just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Meanwhile, can I make sure what you mean by, "we all were dismissed," Witness? I have the question, if you mean every officer or every signatory of the petition? Which was not identical, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regardless of those signatures, we were all collectively dismissed, namely all the policemen were dismissed. So they were all dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, while we are waiting for this to come up, just let me go back to something. You explained that you were no longer under the authorities of Croatia but you continued doing police duties. Whose authority were you under then since you were no longer under the authority of the Croatian MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: While Mr. Slobodan Vujko was there, and I cannot recall the exact date, we worked under the authority of the SUP of the Republic of Croatia, and when he left we no longer were under their jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And whose jurisdiction did you fall under at that point, after you were no longer under the authority of -- under the jurisdiction of the Croatian MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, the SAO Krajina was established and the people were self-organised at that time, as far as I can recall, and as we had all remained jobless, most of us, practically all of us, we were discriminated against by the then Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] That you then came under the authority of the SAO Krajina? Because we just want an answer to that question specifically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, upon its establishment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me -- can I explore this a little bit? Because I think Mr. Knezevic -- it's a little confusing about the dates so let me ask you some specific questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This -- the petition and all that happened in July -- June or July of 1990. The SAO Krajina wasn't established until later, until the beginning of 1991. Also Mr. Vujko was there in the Knin police station until January of 1991. So when -- when was it in relation to those things that you ceased being under the authority of Croatia? That was after the petition, right? In July or August of 1990.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I remember that a telegram came from Zagreb, we received a telegram to the effect that our employment terminated and that referred to all the people working at the SUP Knin. I cannot be sure about the date. I really cannot recall the date. I just remember that there was this telegram about the termination of our employment and the striking us off the payroll and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay but that could have been as late as the beginning of January or the beginning of 1991, you don't -- you can't really recall the date?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Think about it this way and I'll try to get past it, but maybe this question will help. After the barricades went up and the so-called log revolution and all that in the middle of August 1990, whose authority were you under up until the establishment of the SAO Krajina? If you can recall, if you can help us out with that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: In 1990, we were still under the authority of the SUP of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Even after the petition? And even after the log revolution? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes. After the petition for a while, I don't know for how long, I can't remember that, but for some time after the petition as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me show you now this clip that we are able to get ready and it will be on the screen in front of you. If we could all push the e-court button and somebody will come and help you out, Mr. Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This is from Exhibit 4, Your Honour, and then the transcript is Exhibit 5, and this is, I believe, from July of 1990. August, excuse me, 1990. We can play the chip now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, Exhibit 4 is the video and then Exhibit 5 is the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, do you remember ever seeing this on TV at the time? Is this a video that you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No. I have not seen this video ever, this footage on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay, did you hear about Mr. Martic making statements like this at the time in July and August of 1990, about how they no longer were under the authority of Croatia and it was the people's police, things like that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he did make a statement but I cannot tell you when he made that statement. I mean, the exact time. It was quite a long time ago. I don't know when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay but you do remember hearing statement -- hearing statements like that or statements -- hearing about statements like that, whether or not you can tell us the exact time, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I personally did not hear it because I wasn't there. Perhaps he said it, he may have said it, perhaps he was actually seeking to gain some popularity by some statements of his.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. The reason I asked you that question was because you in response to my prior question you'd said, "Well did he make a statement but I cannot tell you when he made that statement." And I just wondered what you meant when you said, well, he did make a statement. Can you explain what it was you were referring to? Was that something that you heard or something that you heard about? Can you just explain, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, believe you me that I never heard him utter a similar statement, because I was a man who was almost all the time in the field doing work in the field, on the ground, and I spent very little time at the police station in Knin proper. And when these statements like the one that you just showed on the video here were given, I cannot confirm that they were uttered in that way because I wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was probably in my native village where I hail from, and where I lived, and that is some 39 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you continued to work at Knin police station, didn't you, according to what you told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you were attending the Knin police station on a daily basis. You had to report for duty every day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you can't then say you were not there unless, if you had gone out on patrol.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is possible, that I had gone out on patrol. I would report for duty and then I would remain there for five or ten minutes and then I would be issued with my daily task and probably go out in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But then when such a momentous statement is made about the group that you belong to, which signed a petition, you don't see, you don't hear it made, and you don't hear about it at all? Nobody mentions it? When you come back to knock off, nobody says, "Hey, Mr. Martic made a statement today to say A, B, C, D"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if I had heard of it, I would say so. I cannot say that I heard or saw something which I didn't see or hear. Your Honours, I did sign that petition but I did not attend this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand you may not have attended this meeting or this occasion when Mr. Martic talked, but I find it a little odd, and I wonder whether you wouldn't agree with me that it is a little odd, that while you worked there, at the police station, you never came to hear of this speech that Mr. Martic made, at the police station, on this very issue, that was so close to your heart. Isn't it odd, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot agree with that. I said what the truth was and the truth is that I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you're not telling the truth. I'm just saying it is a bit odd that you didn't hear about it. It's odd that you didn't hear it specifically. It's even odder, if I can make that comparison -- that degree of comparison, that you didn't hear at all about it. And I'm not questioning your truthfulness. I'm just saying it is funny. But that's fine. You may proceed, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, having now seen the video clip, do Mr. Martic's statements strike you as calming the situation or is it -- isn't it quite the opposite, that this is kind of stirring things up?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In view of your questions and in view of what the Prosecutor has just asked, perhaps it would be a good idea to take a look at the statement again so that he can see whether it was a press conference, whether it was in the police station, whether in the street, whether it was filmed publicly or secretly. Shall we take a look at the clip again, the clip and footage we just saw? Whether Mr. Martic is wearing civilian clothes or uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I don't think any of that stuff matters but let's look at the clip again. I'm happy to watch it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe then the record can show, Mr. Milovancevic, that Mr. Martic is in a blue uniform and it looks like a press conference. Would you agree with that? Would you confirm that, Mr. Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the witness ought to say that, Your Honour. He should tell us what the trousers and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What would you say Mr. Martic is wearing there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's got a denim shirt and I think he's wearing jeans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see the clip again and stop at Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could we freeze the portion where he's in his uniform? Sorry, where he appears in his --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, my pausing skills aren't that great but hopefully this is good enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does that look like, that shirt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a police uniform. It's a denim shirt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you see the person next to him on the right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see the person on the right -- left, oh, yes you're right, on the right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are they not wearing similar shirts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, they are not. The man on the left has a blue shirt. Martic has a denim shirt and jeans, and next to him is Mr. Neso Maric, I know him very well. He's also wearing civilian clothes. And to the right is Mr. Jovan Mitrovic. I don't know who the man on the left is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess it's a question of ipso loquitur.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You're right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, having again seen this, Mr. Knezevic, where Mr. Martic refers to himself as inspector Martic and says they don't support the Croatian authorities and those sorts of things, does that strike you as calming the situation or isn't it really more like kind of stirring up the situation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, I'm not a politician to be competent enough to answer questions like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We understand that you're not an expert or anything like that but your impression is he's not trying to calm things down, he's kind of stirring things up, right? Just your impression.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It is my opinion that Mr. Martic tried to gain something else there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Not to stir the situation up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to have to intervene here. See, you have testified that Mr. Martic was calming the situation, that you were also calming the situation, everybody was calming the situation. Now, you see here a clip in which Mr. Martic is talking about that very situation. Now, I think you don't have to be a politician, you just have to be a human being like you are, look at this clip and be able to say whether or not that looks like calming. You don't need to be a rocket scientist to know that, to make that opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understand what you're asking me but when I said, "calming the situation," I meant when I went to negotiate to Kijevo with my colleague. I'm not talking about this situation with Martic. I was referring to the other situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that clearly but remember you did testify about Mr. Martic. You did tell us that Mr. Martic was an easy going person, very humorous and, of course, there is a bit of humour in what he's saying here, and solving problems, and he was a person who solved difficult problems.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, the question is does that look like solving the problem that had to do with the police at that police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that this was solved in a communist way here, that this is communism. It was said just for the sake of saying something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand you now, when you say it was solved in a communist way. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not, Your Honour, not communist, humorous, humouristic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter heard communist and apologises.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lots of humour in humouristic way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But look at the words he says, the humour we understand in the tone but do those words go to solving the problem? Or do they say, no, we declaring ourselves to be uncooperative now, we are not a Croatian police force, we are these people who -- we are the people's force, what is -- that's what -- those are the words he's using. What do they convey to you as a listener? And what do they convey to the other policemen who are working in that police station and other police stations? Do they convey cooperation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the date of this statement here? Could you tell me that, Mr. Prosecutor? Could you be of assistance? What date are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's sometime after the 18th of August 1990 but I believe still in August 1990. I'm afraid I don't have the exact date on hand, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is there no date on this clip itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Or on the transcript? Can we -- but while we are waiting for the date, sir, I guess you should be able to answer the question without knowing the date. Does -- do the words uttered convey -- what do they convey to you as a listener, if you just came in there and you didn't know anything about this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that someone's interests were in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is that someone and how are they in jeopardy and what interests are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In what way they were in jeopardy, is that the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. And whose interests are these and what interests are they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I meant interests, when I said, "interests," the conduct towards the Serbian people through the HDZ campaign, for instance. Those interests, as far as the Serbian people in the whole of Krajina are concerned, and in the Republic of Croatia. They were -- everything was withheld from them. Our relationship towards the Croatian MUP was not geared towards the state of Croatia and the Croatian people but the Croatian leadership and the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I don't understand how you get that. I'm not asking you to interpret. I'm just asking you what these words convey to you, you know, the words uttered by Mr. Martic themselves. I think it's a very simple question. Shouldn't take us 15 minutes to get the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Martic's statement can be interpreted in two or more ways. And to be quite frank, people interpreted in the way they saw fit. The Croatian side, the Serb side, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question that is being put to you is how do you interpret it? What does it convey to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What it conveys to me is that Mr. Martic was fighting for the interests of the Serb people in Krajina, in this particular case, the police, to protect their rights. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Since you mentioned it just very quickly, how do you think the Croats, the Croat people in the area, would have reacted to this statement of Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's quite logical. You needn't ask me that question. I think that the answer is obvious. If it suited one side, then it wouldn't have suited the other side given the prevailing conditions generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, it may be logical and obvious but the nature of our proceedings here is that I have to ask you questions and you just try your best to answer them so please just go ahead and tell us how Croat people in the area would have reacted to this statement of Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, or rather, Mr. Prosecutor, you should ask the Croatian people or a representative of the Croatian people how they reacted to Mr. Martic's statement. I wasn't in that position, in a position to be able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, but since you're sitting here and even referred to the Croatian side and their interpretation before, I want to move on but before I do I just want to get to you give us your impression of how Croats in the area would have reacted to the statement by Mr. Martic. Would they have been calmed by it or would it have had the opposite affect on them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, the witness should be asked whether the statement was made public and disclosed, who disclosed it, whether the witness had seen it, and then whether it had any public consequences. The witness hasn't told us about any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, if you want to ask those questions in re-examination you'll do so. I don't think you can tell the other side how to ask their questions. You either object to a question because it is objectionable or you wait for -- just wait for me -- or you wait for your turn to clarify those issues that are not clear, and that's a question of clarification. I think I must rule you out of order, please. I'm sorry. I'm sorry, Mr. Milovancevic. I must rule you out of order. Sit down. Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, let's try one more time. I just want to get your impression of how Croats in the area would have reacted to this statement by Mr. Martic. Would they have been calmed by it or would it have had the opposite effect on them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I said a moment ago when you asked me that question that I don't know because I can't -- I'm an Orthodox -- of the Orthodox faith. I can't put my shoes into somebody who is Croatian and tell you that. It depends on the people, on the situation. That's what it all depends on. Because in Knin, in the Knin municipality, there were Croats whom I knew who were no different from us. We were the same, the Orthodox population, the Croatians. Of course, later on when things became more heated it was quite a different matter. But I can't really answer that. Perhaps some of them reacted in one way and others in another way. Some of them might have thought that this raised tensions and other people thought that it was calming the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is it that you can't answer the question or you don't want to answer the question? Because the answer is obvious, as you stated earlier.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not competent enough to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You can't imagine how Croats in the area might have received these words? You just -- you can't recall -- you don't know, you can't imagine, you don't have any opinion on how they might have seen these -- a statement such as this one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they probably wouldn't have supported it. They wouldn't have supported it, the statement. As to anything else, I don't know. I don't know about the other reactions that they might have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me go on. I think we've taken that as far as we can. Are you familiar with the Council for National Resistance which was active in Knin and that area from let's say August 1990 onward?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You never heard of that organisation or that council?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good. I can move on then. When -- I'll try to get through there very quickly because mostly I want to talk to you about 1991 but when barricades were erected on the 17th of August 1990, you your self organised and commanded one of those barricades, correct? Near Knin?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. We said that we wouldn't deal with that topic any more. I tried but wasn't allowed to go ahead. And now the Prosecutor wishes to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black says he withdraws the question. Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yeah. I withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: After August 1990 and into 1991 you became a commander in what was being called Martic's Police, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not become any kind of commander. I just found myself through force of circumstance in the area I was born in, as I was present at the local commune in that time so -- at that time, so that was just through force of circumstance that I happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's not focus I guess on the title or whatever but you found yourself assuming a position of responsibility among this group called -- being called Martic's Police, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't have any responsibility either. And please believe me when I say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you involved in -- well, you were involved, weren't you, in the operation of the training camp in Golubic and now I'm moving into 1991.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Golubic, the camp? Yes. I was there at the training for a period of 21 days, I personally. It was training, not the establishment of a camp. It was just training, training for special units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Sorry if I used the word camp. I didn't mean to be confusing, but we are talking about the same thing. And in Golubic young men came from various places in the Krajina and there they received training in arms and then they went back to their own areas, right? That's the way things worked generally? I think Mr. Martic has a note for his counsel too when there is a chance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, can you help us, please? Mr. Perovic, a note from Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say is this: That Mr. Martic, when the training was underway at Golubic, it was turned into a sort of course or school for the training of policemen because Mr. Martic didn't want to place people in the field who were not trained or who were illiterate or things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I'm correct, right, that people would come from other places in the Krajina, they would come to Golubic to receive training in weapons, and then they would go back to their home towns and villages, that was the pattern, right? I mean not everyone who trained at Golubic was from Golubic or Knin obviously, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: When I was there, they were mostly people from Knin. Later on the camp was abolished as far as I remember. It was closed down after some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, in June 1991, for instance, there were people from many different parts of the Krajina there, in Golubic, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: When I was at the camp, it was the Knin municipality. I don't know about later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When were you at the camp, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1991. In the first stage, and I was among the first people that attended training at the camp. I don't know the exact date but I think it was summertime any way. Or perhaps the spring. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can't remember the month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot, no. I really can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's just about time for our regular break but one quick question before we do in the last 30 seconds. The training at Golubic included various military type training, such as setting mines, preparing ambushes, defending against ambushes, sniper fire, and those types of things, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No. It was how to climb down a slope, down a rope, martial arts, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So nothing about blocking towns or using rifle, grenade launchers or anything like that? That wasn't part of the training? Is that what you're saying? Nothing military?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: While I was there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's time for the regular break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a short break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How much longer do you think you'll be, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm aware of the time and I'm going to speed up as much as I possibly can and, frankly, up till now it's gone much slower than I expected. Some answers were extremely hard to get, but I think I should have no problem finishing today and hopefully with plenty of time for re-examination or questions from Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would be much appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's my intention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We also do have some housekeeping to deal with at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay, thank you. I'll move as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, as you have heard, we want to try to cover a lot of ground quickly. So please if you can just focus on my questions and just try to answer the question I ask you. Just before the break, I was asking you about Golubic and you said that while you were there it was just Knin people although you weren't sure about other times and that there wasn't military training while you were there. I'd like you to look at a document, it's Exhibit 622, and it will come up on the screen in front of you in just a moment. There you can see it, Mr. Knezevic. This document is minutes -- it's in evidence in our case -- it's minutes of a meeting on the morning of 14 June 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours I would note that on the English, the date just has 14, 1991, but on the B/C/S you can see it's clear there is a 6 there so there is just a typo in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You say the English version says 14 what?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The date the first line in the English translation the recording started at 830 hours on 141991 and just the June or 6 is missing, that's all, but it's clear from the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mine has a six.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Oh, really?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, the important part is I'd like you to read that first paragraph, maybe you're already looking at, it says that you attended a meeting with a number of others including Frenki and some others and Captain Dragan. Do you remember this meeting or such a meeting in June of 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't remember this meeting at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But this -- it clearly refers to you here in the first paragraph, right, Dragan Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It does say Dragan Knezevic but there are other Dragan Knezevics so I cannot claim -- I cannot say with certainty that that refers to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But you remember meeting with people like -- you met with Frenki, this refers to Franko Simatovic, correct? You remember meeting with him in 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I only met once with Franko Simatovic at the police station in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about Captain Dragan? You remember meeting with him, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Dragan Karna, is that someone you remember meeting with?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Karna is a colleague who used to work at Sinj and later he was transferred from Sinj to Knin and came to work with us. So I just knew him. I didn't have any concrete dealings with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at the substance of this document and you can tell me whether -- maybe this will remained you of the meeting. If we could scroll down in the B/C/S, please, there is -- it says, it talks about the three objectives of the meeting, and then underlined it says "agreement on further work in Golubic," and what appears there are a number of place names along with numbers, correct? You see where I'm indicating?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In those, those places and the numbers refer to the number of trainees at Golubic from particular locations, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you do not remember ever being at a meeting where it was discussed, trainees from different locations at Golubic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Of this kind, no. Certainly not. I was in charge of leading my eight people from Cetina and Civljani and to train them. As members of a reserve force that would later be placed in the streets to work as policemen. That was my task. As for this meeting, I can guarantee that I wasn't there and I didn't sign this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, yeah, that's -- just so that it's clear I'm not suggesting you signed it. It purports to be minutes. They were typed up after a meeting. So whether you've seen the document is a different thing but you don't recall, you think that you were not in fact at this meeting? It refers to another Dragan Knezevic, is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Possibly, possibly. I certainly did not attend that meeting. I can guarantee that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you just about another part and then we can move on from it. If we turn to the second page in B/C/S, please, and it's page 3 in English, if we could zoom in a bit at the top and Mr. Knezevic there it says 275 firearms need to be given to the areas in the rear towards the Zagrava [phoen] river and Pakrac, then it says, Medak, special training for mining, destruction of roads, luring into ambush and defence from ambush, under Glina and Vojnic, it says, mining of cars, buildings, features, sniper fire, and you can see it continues. Under Plaski, it refers to rifle, grenade-launcher work, ambush. This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, mine has only two pages and what you have been reading, I don't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I suspect maybe I have a different translation, Your Honour, I apologise. There is -- actually I would have another -- it would be at the bottom of page 2, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Page 2 there is nothing at the bottom. There is only three lines on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you see anywhere that it says 270 firearms, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm working on the hard copy. I'll have to check to see if I have a different translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's at page 2 says, Plaski, the construction of defensive position, the blocking of a town, operating with rifle, grenades, ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's the same, Your Honour, and then it's just a few lines before that. Perhaps it's on the prior page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The prior page says, 270 of long barrels are to be given in the area to what's the -- Zagrabija river and Pakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's the same document, Your Honour. Somehow I've come up with a different translation but obviously the one in the system is the one that governs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My question is simply, Mr. Knezevic, in June of 1991, this was the kind of training which was being done at Golubic, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Believe me that I'm not familiar with this. Not with a single segment of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay but putting aside I guess the document whether you're familiar with the document, are you aware that there was this kind of training going on at Golubic in 1991? And if you're not, you can say so or if you just don't know.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me move on to something else, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the number of this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: 212, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, you emphasised earlier in your testimony that there was -- the Croatian MUP established a police station in Kijevo where there had never been one before. First of all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, 622.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The registrar has helped.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. The court officer is keeping me on my game.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, first of all, it was perfectly understandable that they would want to strengthen the police presence in Kijevo because Kijevo found itself between Knin and other Serb villages, right? And tensions were high at the time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a very important at that time but there was no need for 150 policemen to be stationed there. This was -- actually, Kijevo was not endangered at any moment from the people surrounding the area of Kijevo even though they were of a different ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, that may be your opinion but you accept that the people of Kijevo may well have felt afraid, right, under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Actually was the Croatian press and the Croatian media generally that stressed no end the importance -- the importance of Kijevo by stating that if Kijevo fell, that would be the fall of the Alamo and they call Kijevo the Croatian Alamo is and, of course, everyone knows what the significance of the Alamo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But you accept, don't you -- you agree with me that the Croat villagers at Kijevo at the time, they were afraid. They were at least very concerned about their situation under the circumstances, right, and that makes sense, that's understandable?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you were quite right when you say that they were concerned but both sides were concerned the Croats in Kijevo, and the Orthodox folk on the other side were just as concerned seeing what kind of a situation obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay so just focusing on my question you agree with me then that the Croats in Kijevo were concerned, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I agree that they were concerned, but with their redarstvenici, their police force, they had such reinforcement that they actually were creating problems, so that this actually entailed a countereffect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In 1991, Milan Martic appointed you to be the chief of the police in Civljani, correct, to be -- to head up the police there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: There was just a branch office in Civljani of the Knin police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But there had never been a police station or a branch office in Civljani before, had there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It was in fact or there had been a check-point because it borders on the municipalities of Knin and the -- that of Sinj.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But there had never been a police station or a branch office there before, that was something new, right, when you were appointed to head it up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about before. I heard that there was something after the war but I really don't know because after the war that would all be encompassed under Vrlika.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to the earlier question you asked. Do you agree, sir, that Mr. Martic appointed you chief of that police station at that time in Civljani? The question was in 1991, Mr. Milan Martic appointed you to be the chief of the police in Civljani, correct, to be head -- to head up the police there, and you said there was just a branch office in Civljani of Knin police station. You never answered the question put to you. I just want you to answer the question: Were you appointed by Mr. Martic to head the police station in Civljani, whether it was a branch or not a branch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Martic did appoint me but it was just eight people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Doesn't matter how many people. When you got there, did you set it up or had it been an ongoing institution? Did you find a functioning police station when you got there or did you have to start it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was not a police station there, but there were barricades there and Mr. Martic sent us there to take that over, namely not to have untrained people manning them, the peasants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, isn't it the case that you were sort of outraged by a new police presence in Kijevo but it doesn't bother you at all that you had now a new police presence in Civljani? Doesn't that seem like a -- you know, a double standard there on your part?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the police from Knin was also in charge of the local communes of Cetina and Cviljane. There was no need nor the redarstvenici police forces to come to either Kijevo or Civljani but they separated Cetina and Civljani from the Knin municipality when they set themselves up in Kijevo, their police station in Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Whether or not you thought there was a need, the Croatian MUP was perfectly entitled to establish a police presence in any town or village on the territory of Croatia, right? There was nothing unlawful about that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you that there was nothing illegitimate about it but not in so large a number. I don't see why 150 policemen had to be deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: On the 26th of August 1991, the JNA attacked Kijevo together with the SAO Krajina Police, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The JNA attacked Kijevo without the police, because their forces had been attacked at Kosori and Vrlika. Their forces which were in the so-called buffer zone between the Orthodox and Catholic villages, and in that operation, as I indicated earlier, three people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let's focus on the 26th of August 1991. You personally participated in this attack, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I only came to get the prisoners, having been called to do that. And I was called by the duty officer at the Knin police station. That of course can be seen as participation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What time did you arrive in Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: That was sometime in the afternoon, around 3.00 p.m. I cannot be precise, between 3.00 and 4.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Isn't it a fact that Milan Martic was also involved in this and that he had even helped plan and personally was involved in this operation against Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, and I don't know about that. As far as I know, this operation was mounted by the JNA, the army, commanded by General Djukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So as far as you know the police had nothing to do with this other than, like you say, coming to take custody of the captured people, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The police went in after the army to secure the village, but you know or maybe you don't know how one provides security in war conditions, when streets and villages are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You're right. Maybe I don't know. So the police did enter Kijevo on the 26th and they were there still on the 27th of August 1991, correct? Have I understood you correctly? Whether it was, as you say, to secure the village or whether it was part of the actual attack, they were there on the 26th and the 27th of August, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I went back to Knin with the people who were captured at Kijevo and I went back to the police station, i.e., then I went to my brother-in-law's house to spend the night in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So before you arrived around 3.00 p.m., you don't -- you weren't present in Kijevo and then after you went back, after that point whether you took the prisoners, you weren't present in Kijevo either, it was just -- that trip to pick up the prisoners was the only time you were present there, have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you can't -- you have no personal knowledge in fact of anything that happened there before 3.00 p.m., and you don't really know what happened there after you left or on the 27th of August, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know anything that may have happened after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt? When did the police come to Kijevo to secure the place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After this military operation. And that was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that on the 26th of August or on the 27th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether -- whether it was the 26th or the 27th, when these people were taken prisoner at Kijevo. If that was on the 26th, then this was also on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You mean the day you came to take the prisoners from Kijevo to Knin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you to be saying the police arrived there on the same day as you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What time did the police arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they preceded me and I don't know exactly by how long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you cannot say, if indeed -- if this day was the 26th, you cannot say whether they were still there on the 27th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, are you familiar with the ultimatum that was made by Mr. Martic on the 18th of August 1991, to Kijevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I heard that Mr. Martic had made an ultimatum but it was to the police station in Kijevo, that they should get out of there, and he warned the people of the possible consequences in the event any actions took place, because at that time the army was playing the role of peace forces, of negotiators, they agreed that the Kijevo police station should be dismantled, removed, but this was not honoured and then there was the attack at Kosori, at the armed forces, and they actually had to pass through Kijevo to reach their lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did the -- did the Croatian police get out of Kijevo as requested or as demanded by Mr. Martic in the ultimatum? Did they get out before the 26th of August?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. They stayed on, and they were taken prisoner on the 26th, and the rest certainly left, and I can tell you, when I went there to take those prisoners that I did not see a single civilian in Kijevo, not a man, a woman, an elderly person, no one, at least not along the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact, the civilian population of Kijevo fled, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: They had either fled or were resettled by -- on the basis of an agreement. It had to be one of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But you don't know anything about being resettled on the basis of an agreement, you're sort of speculating about that, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Stories were being bandied about that there had been an agreement and with the army, that the army had transported those who wished to go. Not all of them, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, well, let me put it straight to you: Isn't it a fact that the attack on Kijevo had two purposes, to get the Croatian police out and to scare and to drive out the Croatian villagers, the Croat villagers? Weren't those really the purposes, the goals, of the operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I will tell you that your presumption that the goal was to expel the Croatian police, that is correct. But to scare the people off, no, that one isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's -- well maybe -- maybe you didn't see this but when you went to Kijevo in the afternoon of the 26th, did you see that many houses and other civilian buildings had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: When I entered Kijevo, there was just one house by the post office in Kijevo that was on fire, and nothing more. And I believe that house was the so-called Babic house which had been notorious in the Second World War and it was torched by people from Polaca because in 1941, 49 men from Polaca had been slaughtered in the village of Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So who were these people from Polaca? Were they part of the JNA or were they policemen? Or who were these people that torched this particular house, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know. All I heard was that they were people from Polaca, and Bozo Ceko told me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Did you -- did you see that the church, St. Michael's church in Kijevo had been damaged when you were there in the afternoon on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you -- is it that you didn't see the church at all or you saw the church and it wasn't damaged?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I was along the main road, and the church is on the left-hand side up on the hill so you can't see it. It's a kilometre away. I don't know whether it was damaged. I came to Kijevo. It is the Knin-Vrlik-Sinj main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just one last topic, sir. You talked a little bit about Milan Martic's attitude towards Croats and how he dealt with people of different ethnicities. It's true, isn't it, that Milan Martic frequently used the term "Ustasha," both privately and also publicly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, up to 1997 or not [as interpreted], I can guarantee that. Later on, maybe here and there, but you know when you're tired and nervous you come out with all sorts of things but not until 1990, certainly not. Nobody used that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The date we heard was 1997, the first time. Could you just repeat it so that we are clear on what the date was that you mentioned, the year? Maybe you said 1990. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry, it was you know I think it's an interpretation thing or maybe a slip of the tongue on our transcript and in English we heard you said not until 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter meant to say 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Knezevic, the interpreter just corrected this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Everything was over by 1997. That is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Right. That's okay, we have cleared that up. But during 1990 and afterwards, Mr. Martic did use the word Ustasha, right? Both privately and publicly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we didn't have any electricity at that time where we were. We had no electricity at all. I was in the rural areas in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry, if you -- maybe I interrupted you too soon, but do you know whether or not Mr. Martic used the word Ustasha? If you don't know of any occasions, you can say that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I never heard him say that. I personally never ever heard him say that, not on any occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Much of what you testified about here was about Kijevo. You'd agree with me wouldn't you that the attack on Kijevo on the 26th of August had a devastating effect on the villagers of Kijevo; most of them left and any who stayed behind were in very difficult circumstances, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Prosecutor, every move of that kind was terrifying to someone. As to the villagers of Kijevo, they weren't there at all. The elderly and children couldn't have crossed the hill. They took the main road. That's 100 per cent true. If we look towards Kijevo from my area, you have Dinara mountains on one side and on the other, hills, so they certainly couldn't have gone on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So according to you, well, you weren't in Kijevo before 3.00 so you don't really know if there were civilians there when I attack started or not, do you? You can't know that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The army was there before us. Before I arrived in Kijevo, the soldiers were there, the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Right. So you weren't there so you can't say whether the civilian population, the villagers of Kijevo, were present when the attack started or not. I mean, you just don't know, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Boro Djukic told me personally that there was not a single civilian in Kijevo, nor did anybody suffer, there were no casualties, nobody was wounded, there were 62 of --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about after Kijevo? Do you know if there were any villagers who remained after the 26th and 27th? Or was the whole village gone after that? Or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know whether anybody remained in Kijevo. I never went into Kijevo, nor do I know if anybody remained there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you accept, don't you, that -- that Milan Martic was one of the commanders and one of the people who was responsible for the Kijevo operation? Or do you reject that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I am quite convinced that the operation on Kijevo was launched by the JNA. Now, what Martic had to do with and what their relations were I really can't say. And whether they cooperated in any way at all, I can't say. I can't testify about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thanks very much for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. Mr. Milovancevic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Knezevic, the footage that we saw where Mr. Martic was saying something -- well, what we heard here on our monitors?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Right. You remember that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: You mean today? I remember what we saw today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. Now, on that footage, did you see whether it was a public film or let me restate that. Do you see a microphone on any of that footage? Do you remember having seen a microphone anywhere there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: There are no microphones. I didn't see a microphone anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Let me clarify, Mr. Milovancevic, what kind of microphone you mean? You mean such a microphone as in this room, a fixed microphone or a microphone a journalist held in his hand, in his or her hand, and put to Mr. Martic? What kind of microphone do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge, for that question. I meant the microphone that the journalist had, going up to the person he was interviewing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that? Now can that be found on the footage?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: There is none of that on the footage. At least you can't see it on the footage, nothing like that. When I looked at the footage, Rado Zarko told me on one occasion, he was a colleague of mine, that allegedly the lady journalist from one of the newspapers, filmed something secretly. I don't know whether that was the particular footage or not. Heni was her name, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that we see different people on the footage and it's only later on that we hear what Mr. Martic is saying so you -- the voice is separated from the people, the -- on the footage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Need I show the footage again, Your Honour, or is what I'm asking clear enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what you saw, can you tell us which television station filmed what we saw?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: A more general question, was it the Croatian side, Croatian television, or someone else? Can you give us your views on that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume on the basis of what I was able to see, that it was Croatian television. I assume that but I cannot be sure of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Looking at the location, do you think it was an interview with Mr. Martic, was it a press conference, was it a statement made at some public gathering or something else again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It was something else, as far as I was concerned. None of those, something that had nothing to do with a -- it wasn't an interview, it wasn't a public gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now do you remember that the Prosecutor asking you what effect this footage could have had on the Croatian population? Do you remember him asking you that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the following: Can you tell us your opinion about what the television station, the Croatian television, if that is what it was, if it played it to the Croatian population, what was the purpose, what was the goal of showing that to the Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, to raise tensions among the people, to give rise to general panic, to bring about an untoward situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Showing footage of this kind publicly, would that have contributed to fanning the names of interethnic passions or to calming the situation? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it fanned the flames of national passions because the media will be the media. It is the most powerful weapon that exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I didn't want to ask but it's interesting what Mr. Milovancevic now brought up, and may I remind you now of a broadcast about General Spegelj? You remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I do remember it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That was also something quite extreme, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: It was something that was the height of extremity, the most extreme that anybody could have uttered on this planet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Would you say that this statement of General Spegelj was a formal interview or a press conference or a public statement or also something else, as you said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: To be quite frank, it was also something else, and that was secretly filmed, that's for sure. Perpetrated by the services that knew how to do that kind of thing. Services, I'd like to underline. I think it was the KOS at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The final thing -- I didn't understand -- the KOS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Counter-intelligence service of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me, Mr. Milovancevic, I just had to ask this question. You may understand because it may be some parallel, but maybe not. And you had not seen this, what we now saw, these pictures of Mr. Milan Martic? Did I understand you correctly? You don't remember having seen it at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't. Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. But you had a lot of conversations at that time, I suppose, among your colleagues in this difficult days and especially with the people which you mentioned, your friends, among them such friends who had not signed the petition but you were in a constant contact with them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I still maintain contacts with them today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That's nice. And do you think was there any talk at that time about this broadcast on the Croatian TV, presumably Croatian TV?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I now remember that a colleague of mine called Rados Zarko told me that Heni filmed some footage secretly. Now, I can't be sure whether he meant this footage or something else. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. Now to the more general question I wanted to ask you. When you -- it deals with Kijevo. Did I understand you correctly, you said you came in after the police but you didn't stay there, you came between 3.00 and 4.00 p.m. or so, in order to take these prisoners to Knin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. About 3.00. I can't be specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And how did you then manage taking these prisoners to Knin and where in Knin did you bring them to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll repeat that. They were lined up next to the old local office along the road. 40 people got into the bus. It was a Jadran Trans company bus transporting passengers along that route. I and Ceko Boro [as interpreted] escorted them to the police station in Knin. Whereas the other 20 left with a military bus, a small military bus, and they were transported by the army in that small bus of theirs. They were taken over to the police station in Knin. I don't know who was the duty officer. And then later on they were transported to the south barracks and exchanged. That's what I heard and that's the truth of it. Of the 40, which we brought to Knin, not a hair of their head was harmed while they were there in the bus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: They were regarded prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Do you know the detention facility which was set up in the old hospital of Knin?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No. All I know is that the people slept there, nothing more than that. Not about any detention facility, prison. They slept there, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And then something, a final question. Maybe you know this person from Golubic or from somewhere else. Do you know Stevo Plejo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Stevo Plejo? Possibly, but the name doesn't ring a bell now. I might recognise him if I saw him. I might know the face.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I just have a few questions for you. Now, in respect of the 21 day training at Golubic, during the time, did you learn or were you instructed in anything more than climbing down a slope, climbing down a rope, and martial arts? Was that the full extent of your training?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So you received training at a later time, additional training? And if yes, what was it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Zagreb I attended and graduated from the secondary school of internal affairs. We had martial arts which we trained our young generation in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No. I mean after the training in Golubic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you a bit about the persons who did training with you. What ages were they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: There was something about young men, he said, I remember, and I didn't -- that -- that didn't say too much actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What were their ages? Are you able to recall? Were they in their 40s, 18 or 19 year olds or what was it that you recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: They were mostly people between 20 and 24, not older than that. One or two might have been old -- slightly older but most of them were that age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: These people were trained and then they would join a unit, that's correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly in the police force, but usually with older colleagues who were more experienced. They weren't allowed to work on their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could you tell me what sort of uniform you would wear?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I had a police uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please describe it for me, including any insignia and any headgear, fully.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: In Golubic? Or while I was training or generally?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Both when you were at Golubic and then afterwards.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Golubic, it was a camouflage uniform and a beret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Any emblem or insignia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, we didn't have any insignia. I didn't have an emblem or insignia. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Nothing at all on this camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have anything, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Anything on the beret? I beg your pardon. I didn't put on my microphone. Anything on the beret?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I think that there was the Yugoslav tricolour on the beret, the flag of the former Yugoslavia, three-coloured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, what about after?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: The tricolour remained until the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: When you say the end.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Until later, until later. The witness said, "until later."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Later meaning when?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was there until 1993. After that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And up to that point, your uniform remained the same as you have just described or did it change?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, they were camouflage, blue camouflage uniforms. People who went in the field. The people who were in town, they had the normal type of police uniform, a shirt, trousers and the Titovka-type cap, not the Satka-type cap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What was the colour of that uniform? And what if anything was on the cap?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: There was the three-coloured Yugoslav flag on the cap, nothing more than that. Perhaps somebody might have placed something else of their own accord but the official cap had the three-coloured flag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Was there any insignia on your uniform itself? Any badge, any patch? You seem to have to think harder.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: No. It's not that I'm thinking hard. I know what you're asking me. There was the militia or police of SAO Krajina; SAO Krajina is what it said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And you began wearing that uniform when?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. I don't know. I don't know the date when we started wearing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now I want you to cast your mind back. You mentioned Knin and you said in respect of the -- should I repeat? In respect of the Knin police station, you would go in, report for duties for five minutes, receive your assignment, and then leave. You would leave for beat duties in Knin or outside of Knin? Or where would you leave for, having got your assignment usually?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, beat patrol.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Where I'm asking. Where would it be?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the territory of Knin municipality. We would regulate traffic and go out on patrols, on beats, Kistanje, Erdvenit [phoen], Strmica, Kosovo, Civljani, Polaca, Biskupija, all those directions. We covered the whole area. We would go to one area one day, to another the next day, depending on where they sent us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Right. Now, there is a final area I'm going to touch on. You recall having given evidence in respect of -- one moment, please -- the prisoners which were for exchange, and Mr. Martic came to inspect them, and he told us, "Please make sure none of these people are harmed or killed." And your colleague, I think it was Bozo Ceko, asked why, and Mr. Martic said, "Well, they have to be exchanged." Do you know why Mr. Martic said that to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I do. Bozic, and his cousin, Vaso Pecir, was killed in May and Bozo Ceko was angry about that, and the two of us took them to Knin, to the police station. So that's why, to prevent the man reacting in a way he shouldn't react. And Bozo Ceko was in prison in Zagreb, so he was angry at everyone. That's why Martic said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So Mr. Martic had a fear that - is it Bozo Ceko? - might do some physical harm or injury to the prisoners? And he was issuing a caution that because they had to be exchanged, you had to be careful as to the condition they were in? And ensure that no harm befell these particular prisoners? Is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: Not only because of that. That was standard practice with us, when anything like that happened. Of course, we didn't take many prisoners. There weren't many operations like that. Mostly the population left before the action took place so there was no capturing, either on our side, the Orthodox side, or the Catholic side, the Croatian side. The same would have applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. What was standard practice?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what you mean, what do you mean by standard practice. You said not only that, that was standard practice with us or something like that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN KNEZEVIC
utterances.text: I meant to -- that the conduct towards the prisoners had to be according to the Geneva Conventions. That's what I meant. That was the practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
